newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot power mostly up amid higher demand.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot power mostly up amid higher demand.

text.p: Spot power prices in the western U.S. rose amid expected higher demand in both the Southwest and Northwest, where a storm is expected to hit later today, markets sources said Wednesday.
"Daily prices at COB (California-Oregon border) should come off after the storm," said one utility trade source.
In addition, tight marginal supplies of natural gas and higher spot gas prices are keeping western power prices firm.
Industry sources mentioned the unplanned outage of a coal-fired power plant in the Northwest as contributing to the market tightness, but this could not be confirmed.
They also noted rain in the Northwest is not expected to add to hydroelectric generation, while dam operations could be curtailed for flood control purposes.
Nevertheless, market sources said heavy storms in the Northwest, which have created deep snowpack, are bearish for the long-term market since the spring runoff will likely be above normal.
Firm, peak COB electricity for Thursday was assessed at $33.00-34.00 per megawatt hour (MWH), up from $29.25-29.75 on Tuesday.
Firm, off-peak COB power for Thursday was quoted $19.00-20.00, compared with $17.00-18.00.
Next-day firm, peak power at Mid-Columbia (Mid-C) was quoted $31.00-32.00, compared with Tuesday's $27.50-29.50.
Thursday firm, off-peak power at Mid-C was higher at $18.00-19.00.
Firm, peak Palo Verde (PV) electricity for Thursday was quoted $27.00-28.00 per megawatt hour (MWh), little changed from Wednesday. Firm, off-peak PV power was higher at $18.00-19.00.
Next-day firm, peak prices at Four Corners were quoted $28.00-29.00 per MWh, also little changed. Off-peak Four Corners was assessed near $18.00.
